questions.question: How does http.ListenAndServe work in Go?
questions.title: Http Listenandserve
questions.direct_answer: http.ListenAndServe(addr, handler) starts an HTTP server on the address with the given handler (nil = DefaultServeMux). It blocks until the server errors or shuts down.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: http.ListenAndServe(addr, handler) starts an HTTP server on the address with the given handler (nil = DefaultServeMux). It blocks until the server errors or shuts down.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The one-line server:

```bash
func main() {
    http.HandleFunc("/", handler)
    http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil)
}
```

The two arguments: the address (\":8080\" binds all interfaces; ":0" picks a port), and the handler (nil = http.DefaultServeMux — the global router that HandleFunc registers into).

What happens inside: ListenAndServe creates an http.Server, calls net.Listen("tcp", addr) to bind, then Serve(listener) — the accept loop. Each accepted connection gets a goroutine that reads the request, routes it through the handler, and writes the response. One goroutine per connection — that's Go's concurrency model directly applied to HTTP.

Executed (via httptest — the same machinery without a real port):
```go
mux := http.NewServeMux()
mux.HandleFunc("/hello", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    fmt.Fprintln(w, "hello")
})
// GET /hello → 200 "hello" — verified
```

What ListenAndServe returns: an error — and it's always non-nil (it returns when the server stops: a bind error (port in use), a Close call, or a Serve error. That's why the idiom is `log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(...))` — the error is the exit.

The production form: http.Server gives you the knobs (timeouts, TLS, graceful shutdown):
```go
srv := &http.Server{
    Addr:         ":8080",
    ReadTimeout:  10 * time.Second,
    WriteTimeout: 30 * time.Second,
    Handler:      mux,
}
srv.ListenAndServe()
```

For tests, http.Server is the same thing with an httptest listener — no port, no network.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    LS[ListenAndServe addr handler] --> L[net.Listen bind] --> A[Accept loop]
    A --> SP[go handle conn] --> R[parse request] --> H[find handler] --> W[write response]
    A --> A
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The Serve loop, one layer down: for { conn := listener.Accept(); go srv.newConn(conn) } — accept, spawn, repeat. Each connection goroutine parses the HTTP (headers, body framing), builds the *http.Request, finds the handler (ServeMux pattern matching), calls it with (ResponseWriter, Request), and closes. The concurrency IS the goroutine-per-connection — no thread pool to size, no event loop to configure.

The nil handler means DefaultServeMux — a package-level global router. HandleFunc registers into it. The global is convenient for small programs and a dependency concern for large ones (any package can register; the route table is global mutable state) — which is why production code creates its own ServeMux and passes it explicitly.

The timeout story interviewers probe: ListenAndServe with no Server sets NO timeouts — a slow client can hold a connection forever (Slowloris-class attacks). The production Server struct's ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout/IdleTimeout are the defense — and the zero-value-usable philosophy means the simple form works until you need the hardening, then the explicit Server is there.
